title: GPTSwarm: Language Agents as Optimizable Graphs
mutable_substrate: Two levels: node-local LLM prompts and directed communication edges between node/agent graphs; internal agent topology is fixed in the reported structural optimizer.
optimization_operator: REINFORCE with Adam over Bernoulli edge-inclusion logits subject to DAG constraints; iterative node-prompt improvement from execution histories, instantiated with demonstration selection and UCB1 in experiments.
feedback_selection: Task-specific scalar utilities: MMLU correctness, Mini Crosswords best-state word accuracy (with a 0.4 baseline shift), and unit-test pass/fail for HumanEval demonstration selection. GAIA uses prompt-based self-consistency or best-answer selection without graph optimization.
archive_memory: Each node stores an execution history h_n of local inputs, predecessor context, outputs, and optional quality annotations. HumanEval uses the ten most recent node inputs and at most four demonstrations; there is no cross-run population archive of graph programs.
validation_strategy: Sample graphs from the learned distribution and evaluate on benchmark problems; report multiple seeds/runs where affordable, matched-edge-density ablations on Mini Crosswords, dense/random topology controls on MMLU, and full-dataset evaluation after HumanEval updates.
adaptation_mode: Primarily offline task-level topology search, with demonstrated cross-model transfer of a learned topology; HumanEval also evaluates continuous online node-prompt adaptation without resetting.
benchmarks: MMLU adversarial and collaborative multi-agent question answering
principal_results: Edge optimization restores truthful single-agent-level MMLU performance in swarms containing equal numbers of truthful and adversarial agents.
Role-diverse MMLU swarms improve the single-agent baseline by 2.1% ± 1.1% across five seeds.
Mini Crosswords improves from 0.465 ± 0.0509 to 0.575 ± 0.0275 after edge optimization; subsequent node optimization reaches 0.668 ± 0.0060.
A learned Mini Crosswords distribution optimized with GPT-3.5-Turbo reaches 0.800 ± 0.0616 with GPT-4-Turbo, versus 0.668 for the rerun TOT baseline.
HumanEval online node optimization improves accuracy from 0.76 to 0.88 ± 0.007.
A seven-TOT-agent GAIA swarm averages 18.45, versus 9.70 for GPT-4-Turbo, but GAIA does not use edge or node optimization.
On adversarial MMLU, GPTSwarm reaches 0.8301 versus DyLAN's 0.8366 while using far lower optimization and inference cost.
limitations: Only inter-agent communication edges are structurally optimized; internal node topology is fixed.
The all-pairs cross-agent candidate set grows quadratically and scaling beyond 100 agents is unresolved.
Graph utilities are benchmark-specific and may invite overfitting or evaluator gaming; held-out robustness is limited.
Several expensive results use only one transferred graph distribution or few repetitions.
Hosted preview LLMs, search APIs, and historical pricing reduce exact reproducibility.
GAIA demonstrates composition rather than automatic optimization, so it does not validate self-improving general-purpose tool use.
safety_controls: Hard DAG constraint prevents cyclic execution in the optimized graph.
Adversarial-agent experiment shows task-utility-driven pruning of harmful information channels.
No explicit alignment, sandboxing, capability control, evaluator-robustness, or safe-release mechanism is implemented.

explicit_predecessors.name: Society of Mind / Natural-Language Societies of Mind
explicit_predecessors.evidence: GPTSwarm adopts modular, hierarchical intelligence and represents societies of agents as composite graphs.

explicit_predecessors.name: Graph of Thoughts
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper generalizes graph-structured prompting to agents that also contain tools, function calls, and other operations.

explicit_predecessors.name: DSPy
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Both represent LLM pipelines as computational graphs; GPTSwarm replaces Cartesian-product prompt search with iterative node-wise updates conditioned on execution history.

explicit_predecessors.name: OPRO and PromptBreeder
explicit_predecessors.evidence: They motivate using LLM-driven improvement as the generic node optimizer I.

explicit_predecessors.name: DyLAN
explicit_predecessors.evidence: DyLAN heuristically scores and prunes agents, while GPTSwarm learns edge probabilities and compares accuracy and cost on adversarial MMLU.

explicit_predecessors.name: STOP
explicit_predecessors.evidence: STOP jointly optimizes prompts and inference structure through a self-applied improver; GPTSwarm instead separates node prompts from graph-edge optimization.

explicit_predecessors.name: REINFORCE
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The edge optimizer uses its score-function gradient estimator over sampled DAGs.

open_questions: Can internal agent topology be added, removed, and rewired jointly with cross-agent communication?
How can candidate edges and credit assignment scale to hundreds or millions of agents?
When do learned graph distributions transfer across tasks, datasets, tools, and model families?
How should held-out evaluators and safety constraints prevent reward hacking during online adaptation?
Can prompt and edge optimization be performed jointly without unstable coupled updates?
What optimization budget is required before gains amortize their monetary, token, and latency cost?
How can a swarm preserve role diversity and avoid convergence to redundant or brittle routes?
